1.text: THE ceremonials of the Chukchee, as said before, have for their chief

2.text: purpose the protection of the material welfare of the family. Most of them

3.text: form a yearly cycle, recurring from season to season with befitting changes.

4.text: The reindeer-breeders and the maritime people have their separate cycles

6.text: CEREMONIALS OF THE REINDEER CHUKCHEE. — The Reindeer Chukchee,

7.text: in their ceremonials, differentiate those that are connected with the reindeer-

8.text: herd from all others, and call them “sacrifices” (taaroˊng̣ɪrg̣ɪt) or “genuine

9.text: sacrifices” (lɪˊê-taaroˊng̣ɪrg̣ɪt). Their essential feature is the slaughtering of

10.text: reindeer for sacrifice. These are the only ceremonials that are considered to

11.text: belong to the regular cycle.¹ The other ceremonials refer to various subjects,

12.text: such as giving thanks for success in hunting, the fulfilment of orders received

13.text: in dreams, engaging in ceremonial sports, etc.

14.text: I shall observe the above distinction in describing the ceremonials, though

15.text: I consider some of the second class fully as important as those of the first.

16.text: For instance, the ceremonial of giving thanks for success in hunting is con-

17.text: spicuous among the ceremonials celebrated by the Maritime Chukchee and

18.text: the Eskimo. It is likewise very important in the life of the Reindeer Chukchee,

19.text: and is accompanied by sacrifices, but they are of only secondary importance.

20.text: The ceremonials connected with birth and death, which are similar among

21.text: the reindeer-breeders and the maritime people, will be described in a separate

23.text: Strictly speaking, every slaughtering of reindeer is a sacrifice, and is

24.text: performed according to certain rules. After the animal is stabbed, the Chuk-

25.text: chee watch carefully to see on which side it falls. To fall on the wounded

26.text: side is a less favorable omen than to fall on the other; and to fall backwards

27.text: is still worse, and forebodes misfortune. The man who holds the halter often

28.text: tries by a dexterous jerk to make the animal fall in a favorable position.

29.text: The carcass is pointed with its head in the direction which is to receive the

30.text: sacrifice, and a small branch of stunted willow is put under the hind-quarters

31.text: to serve as bedding. Then blood is taken from the wound and sprinkled, first

32.text: in the direction toward which the offering is made, then in other directions.

33.text: The antlers are cut away, together with the top of the skull, and the carcass

34.text: is then ready to be skinned and cut up.
